opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most underappreciated problems in the field. A lot of our benchmarks are borrowed straight from the machine learning playbook—you hold out a test set, measure correlation with some assay, and report a number. But a model can score really well on those metrics without understanding anything we'd actually call biology. It can lean on evolutionary statistics, exploit homology leakage between train and test, or pick up on quirks of how a dataset was collected.

So the question I keep coming back to is: what would actually convince a skeptical biologist? For me it's whether the model generalizes in the directions that matter—out of distribution, to the parts of sequence or phenotype space where the training data is sparse. A model that's truly learned the underlying rules should hold up when you move away from what it's seen, not just interpolate within it.

The other piece is that the ultimate evaluation is experimental. The honest benchmark for a lot of this work isn't a leaderboard; it's whether the model's predictions hold up when you go test them at the bench. That's expensive and slow, which is exactly why people avoid it, but it's the thing that separates a model that's memorized correlations from one that's captured real mechanism. I'd love for the field to invest much more in prospective, wet-lab-validated evals rather than yet another retrospective split.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest starting point is that most of the benchmarks we have in biology right now are really tests of recall, not understanding. You can ask a model a multiple-choice question that looks like it came off a graduate qualifying exam, it gets ninety-something percent, and everyone gets excited. But that's measuring whether the model has seen the textbook. It tells you almost nothing about whether it can do biology.

So when we think about evaluation, the first thing I push on is: what would a good postdoc actually be able to do that a bad one couldn't? And a lot of that is not knowing facts. It's knowing what experiment to run next. It's looking at a messy dataset and recognizing that the effect you're seeing is probably a batch artifact rather than real signal. It's saying, "This result is too clean, something's wrong with the controls." Those are judgment calls, and they're where expertise actually lives.

The second thing is that biology is a wet-lab science, and ultimately the ground truth is a result that comes out of an experiment. That gives you a real advantage over a lot of other domains, because you can close the loop. You can ask a model to design a guide RNA, or predict which variants of a protein will fold and bind, or propose a perturbation that should produce a particular phenotype, and then you can go test it. The eval isn't "did you match the reference answer." The eval is "did the thing you proposed work in cells." That's expensive and slow compared to running a benchmark on a cluster, but I think it's the only evaluation that really counts, and the cost is coming down fast as automation gets better.

Third, I try to be careful about contamination in a way that's specific to biology. The literature is enormous and highly redundant, so if you build an eval from published results, a strong model has almost certainly seen some version of it. What's more interesting is held-out data, meaning experiments where the result exists but hasn't been published yet, or where you generate the data specifically for the eval. We've done versions of this where we run the experiment, hold the result, ask the model to predict it, and then compare. That's the closest thing I've found to a genuinely fair test.

And then the last piece, which is a little more philosophical, is that I think we should be asking models to be wrong in the right way. A good scientist doesn't just produce correct predictions, they produce calibrated ones. They know when they don't know. If a model confidently predicts the outcome of an experiment where the honest answer is "this is genuinely uncertain, here are the two plausible outcomes and here's the experiment that would distinguish them," that's a failure even if it happens to guess right. So I'd love to see more evaluations that reward well-reasoned uncertainty, and penalize fluent confidence that isn't earned. That's a harder thing to score, but it's much closer to what we actually want from a scientific collaborator.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start by asking what you mean by biological understanding. Is it knowing the literature? Is it predicting what happens when you perturb a system? Or is it being able to design an experiment that distinguishes between two competing explanations? Those are very different capabilities, and a model can be good at one without being good at the others.

For me, a compelling evaluation would be prospective. Give the model a biological problem where the answer hasn’t been measured yet, ask it to make a prediction, and then test that prediction experimentally. You want to hold out enough of the biological context that success requires generalization—maybe a different cell type or a combination of perturbations it hasn’t seen.

But I’d also evaluate the process. Does it identify the right controls? Does it recognize when the data are insufficient? Can it propose an experiment that would actually change its mind? Biology is full of situations where several explanations fit the same observation. Being able to articulate a plausible story is a much lower bar than being able to tell those explanations apart.

So I’d want an evaluation loop: prediction, experiment, new evidence, revision. Can the model help us learn something reliable about a biological system with fewer experiments? That’s a much more meaningful measure than whether it can answer a difficult biology exam question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between knowing facts about biology and being able to reason about a biological system. A model can do very well on an exam because it has seen a lot of similar questions. That’s useful, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it can help you discover something new.

So I’d like evaluations where the model has to make a prediction about an experiment it hasn’t seen. If you perturb a gene in a particular cell type, what happens? Can it predict when the answer changes in a different cellular context? And can it tell you where it’s uncertain?

Then you want to close the loop with experiments. Ask the model to propose hypotheses, choose experiments that distinguish between them, and update its predictions when the results come back. Biology is full of results that surprise us. How a model responds to that surprise is a much stronger test than whether it can give a convincing explanation after the fact.

Ultimately, the question is whether using the model helps us learn something reliable about biology that we wouldn’t otherwise have learned, or get there with fewer experiments. That’s the kind of capability I’d want an evaluation to measure.
